main_damage_causes: Sirius Black's sole appearance in the Book 1 corpus — his motorcycle loan and his name-drop by Hagrid — is completely excised from the film, removing his foreshadowing as a trusted member of the Potter inner circle from the saga's opening scene.
The film provides no establishment of Sirius as a figure connected to the events of Halloween night 1981, meaning his later importance to Harry's story has no narrative seed in the adaptation.

The corpus for both book and film is heavily weighted toward material in which Sirius does not appear directly, so most damage is confined to this one omitted reference rather than any active mischaracterization of Sirius on screen.
Sirius Black does not appear in either the book corpus or the film corpus provided — both corpora cover Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets, in which Sirius Black plays no role
Without any corpus evidence of Sirius Black's portrayal in either the book or film sections provided, no damaging scenes can be identified per the anti-hallucination rules

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 1 — Hagrid delivers Harry to Privet Drive
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, Hagrid tells Dumbledore and McGonagall that 'Young Sirius Black lent it to me' (the motorcycle), establishing Sirius as a named, trusted figure in the Potter inner circle from the very first chapter. Hagrid also states he will return the bike to Sirius: 'I'll be takin' Sirius his bike back.' This is the saga's first reference to Sirius, planting him as someone close enough to lend his prized possession and integrated into the events of Halloween night.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film's opening scene shows Hagrid arriving on the motorcycle with no mention of Sirius Black whatsoever. There is no line about who lent him the bike, no name-drop, no establishment of Sirius as a figure connected to this night. Sirius is entirely absent from the narrative setup of the saga's opening.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's first chapter plants Sirius Black as a trusted insider of the Order and a close friend of the Potters before the reader even meets Harry. His motorcycle — a personal, memorable possession — being lent to Hagrid for this mission signals his active participation in protecting Harry on the night Voldemort fell. Removing this reference means film audiences have zero foreshadowing of Sirius and no early sense of his relationship to Harry's history. When Sirius becomes central to the third film, there is no retroactive resonance from this founding moment. The relationship between Sirius and Hagrid, and Sirius's place in the original circle of trust around Dumbledore, is entirely absent from the film adaptation's foundation.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 29 (Shrieking Shack) — Lupin's opening line to Black
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, Lupin enters the Shrieking Shack with his wand raised, looking bloodless and frightened, and immediately asks 'Where is he, Sirius?' — his reunion with Black is one of dawning understanding, not hostility. His first words to Black are purposeful and searching.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Lupin enters and delivers the taunting line 'Looking a bit ragged, aren't we, Sirius? Finally the skin reflects the madness within.' This frames Lupin as briefly adversarial and mocking, before pivoting to the embrace — creating a false beat of condemnation toward Black.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's reunion carries no performative hostility from Lupin — he is tense and urgent, not cruel. The film's taunt momentarily paints Black as truly appearing monstrous to an old friend, slightly undermining the warmth of the friendship being revealed. Minor but distorts the dynamic of their reunion.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 29 (Shrieking Shack) — Black's 'He dies. Now.' urgency and characterization as unhinged
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, Black is desperate and hollowed but coherent. He agrees to let Lupin explain ('Tell them whatever you like. But make it quick, Remus. I want to commit the murder I was imprisoned for.') — dark humor intact, but he defers to Lupin's insistence on explanation. He is driven, not purely demented.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Black snarls 'Yes, you glow like the sun. And you howl at the moon. Enough talk! He dies. Now. If you won't do it with me, Remus, I'll do it alone.' and 'I did my waiting! Twelve years of it! In Azkaban! Trust me, you wouldn't have lasted a week!' — presented as borderline unhinged and taunting, with no dark wit or reluctant patience.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's Black is terrifying but controlled enough to be persuasive and even darkly witty. The film reduces him to feral screaming and bravado, making him harder to sympathize with at the moment the audience most needs to begin believing him. His intelligence and the complexity of his fury — righteous but disciplined enough to yield to Lupin — is flattened.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 29 (Shrieking Shack) — Black's accusation scene compressed; Harry's agency and confrontation reduced
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book devotes extensive space to Harry physically attacking Black — lunging at him, punching him, choking him with hatred — before ultimately holding the wand at Black's heart and choosing not to kill him. This is a defining moral moment for Harry: he has the power, the rage, and the justification, and he still hesitates. Harry's internal struggle ('Now was the moment to do it... The seconds lengthened. And still Harry stood frozen') is the emotional climax of his arc.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film compresses this entirely. Harry raises his wand and says 'Yes' when asked if he's going to kill Black, but there is no physical assault, no extended confrontation, no frozen moment of choice. The scene cuts almost immediately to Lupin's entrance. Harry never has the sustained, agonizing moment of choosing mercy.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's Shrieking Shack climax is built around Harry's choice not to kill — it defines his moral character as distinct from revenge, and mirrors his father's legacy of mercy (James once saved Snape). By eliminating the physical confrontation and the long frozen moment, the film removes Harry's most significant moral decision in the entire book. His mercy toward Pettigrew later therefore lacks the full weight it should carry, since the audience hasn't seen how close he came to acting on his rage.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 29 (Shrieking Shack) — Pettigrew confrontation: Black and Lupin's moral speech compressed
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book gives Black a powerful, extended speech condemning Pettigrew: 'THEN YOU SHOULD HAVE DIED! DIED RATHER THAN BETRAY YOUR FRIENDS, AS WE WOULD HAVE DONE FOR YOU!' and 'What was there to be gained by fighting the most evil wizard who has ever existed? Only innocent lives, Peter!' These speeches define Black's moral code — loyalty above survival — and are among his most important characterization moments in the series.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film condenses this to 'Died! Died rather than betray my friends! And you should have realized, Peter, if Voldemort didn't kill you... we would.' The moral elaboration — the specific condemnation of cowardice, the statement about what was worth fighting for — is absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Black's extended condemnation of Pettigrew is one of the clearest windows into his values: he believes in absolute loyalty and considers cowardice in the face of evil to be unforgivable. This shapes how the audience understands him as a moral actor, not merely a wronged man. The compression loses his voice and his ethical core at a critical moment.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 30 (Whomping Willow exterior) — Sirius comforting Lupin during transformation
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book does not feature Black attempting to comfort Lupin during transformation. Black transforms into the dog immediately to try to protect everyone, and the transformation is chaotic. There is no tender moment of Black holding Lupin and speaking to his humanity.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film adds a scene where Black wraps his arms around the transforming Lupin and speaks: 'You know the man you truly are, Remus. This flesh is only flesh. This heart is where you truly live. This heart! Here!' — a sentimental, invented beat.
damaging_scenes.explanation: While this scene adds warmth to the Black-Lupin friendship, it is not in the corpus and slightly softens Black into a nurturing figure in a way that is tonally inconsistent with his book characterization, which is more fierce and action-oriented. It also delays the transformation scene in a way that strains credibility. The damage is minor but real — it imposes a sentimentality on Black not established in the source.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 30 (Whomping Willow) — Pettigrew's escape; Black's response
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, when Pettigrew escapes, Black immediately scrambles up and chases him as a dog, bleeding from the werewolf fight. He is driven and purposeful despite his wounds — 'Black was bleeding; there were gashes across his muzzle and back, but at Harry's words he scrambled up again, and in an instant, the sound of his paws faded to silence as he pounded away across the grounds.'
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film has Harry cast Expelliarmus to stop Pettigrew, and Pettigrew transforms himself and escapes. Black — still as a dog — is then thrown by the werewolf. The agency of pursuit is transferred away from Black, and his chase of Pettigrew is absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: In the book, Black's pursuit of Pettigrew even while wounded demonstrates his relentless commitment to the mission that drove his escape from Azkaban. The film eliminates this entirely — Pettigrew simply escapes during the chaos, and Black never actively gives chase. This reduces Black from an agent pursuing justice to a passive victim of circumstance in the final act.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 18 (Three Broomsticks) — Overheard conversation: godfather revelation given to Harry as emotional climax
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, the revelation that Black is Harry's godfather lands as one beat among many in the Hogsmeade conversation — important, but part of a longer backstory. Harry's emotional response is internal and complex, mixing hatred with something harder to name. The scene ends with Harry lying awake with a 'boiling hatred' and fantasizing about Black's betrayal.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film makes the godfather reveal the emotional climax of the scene, delivered last by McGonagall with dramatic weight ('Sirius Black was and remains today... Harry Potter's godfather.'). Harry then emerges weeping on a rocky outcrop and delivers: 'I hope he finds me. But when he does, I'm going to be ready. When he does, I'm going to kill him.' This is a scripted, performed declaration that simplifies Harry's roiling internal conflict into a clean revenge statement.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's Harry doesn't make a clean declaration of intent to kill — he is confused, full of hatred he can barely contain, but also uncertain ('He didn't know what he wanted to do'). The film's Harry is resolved and declarative. This simplification removes the moral ambiguity that makes his later choice not to kill Black so meaningful. If the audience believes Harry definitively planned to kill Black, his mercy reads as a change of heart; in the book, it reads as the resolution of genuine internal conflict.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 41 (Sky/Hogwarts) — Sirius's farewell speech to Harry
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, Black's farewell in the tunnel is intimate and tentative: he hesitantly offers Harry a home ('I'll understand, of course, if you want to stay with your aunt and uncle. But... well... think about it. Once my name's cleared... if you wanted a... a different home...'), and Harry's enthusiasm ('Are you insane? Of course I want to leave the Dursleys!') produces Black's first true smile — 'the difference it made was startling, as though a person ten years younger were shining through the starved mask.' The final parting on the tower is brief: 'We'll see each other again. You are — truly your father's son, Harry.'
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film replaces this with an invented inspirational speech: 'Trust yourself. No matter the challenges you face — and I fear they will be many — you'll be surprised how many times you can find the answers... here' (tapping his heart). This is generic mentor-speak that doesn't belong to Black's characterization.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's farewell is powerful precisely because of its specificity: the tentative offer of a home, Harry's explosive eagerness, and Black's smile transforming his ruined face. It establishes the Black-Harry bond as one of mutual need and genuine warmth rooted in James Potter's memory. The film replaces this with a generic inspirational homily that could have been spoken by any mentor character. Black's distinctive voice — wary, scarred, tentatively hopeful — is erased at the most important bonding moment of their relationship.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 29 (Shrieking Shack) — Black's explanation of how he escaped Azkaban and found Pettigrew absent
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book contains Black's extended explanation of his escape: that knowing he was innocent kept him sane (not a happy thought the dementors could feed on), that he transformed into a dog to slip through the bars, and that seeing Pettigrew in the Daily Prophet photograph gave him the obsessive purpose to escape. This explanation is a crucial character moment — it shows Black's intelligence, resilience, and the particular nature of his survival.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film does not include Black's explanation of his Azkaban escape or how he identified Pettigrew. The clipping is shown briefly, but Black's internal account of what kept him sane and how he escaped — one of the most revealing passages in the book for his characterization — is entirely absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Black's Azkaban escape is not just plot — it reveals that his innocence itself was his weapon, that he retained a sense of self where others lost theirs, and that his love for Harry (the obsession to protect him from Pettigrew) gave him the strength to act. Without this, the audience doesn't understand how Black survived twelve years with his mind intact, nor how his escape connects to his devotion to James Potter's memory and Harry's safety. His survival reads as merely convenient rather than a testament to character.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 4 (Leaky Cauldron) — Mr. Weasley's warning to Harry: 'Why would I go looking for someone who wants to kill me?'
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, Harry overhears the Weasley argument and learns the truth about Black secondhand — he is not told directly by Mr. Weasley. When Harry finally speaks to Mr. Weasley about it, Harry demonstrates that he is not frightened in the expected way and is more bothered about missing Hogsmeade than about the threat to his life. His reaction to the Black threat is notably un-panicked and self-possessed.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film has Mr. Weasley tell Harry directly that Black escaped to kill him, and Harry's response — 'Mr. Weasley, why would I go looking for someone who wants to kill me?' — is played for a mild laugh and positions Harry as sensibly passive from the outset. This predisposes the audience to see Harry as unlikely to pursue Black.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's Harry is more internally conflicted about Black from earlier — he overhears the truth, processes it alone, and is conspicuously not panicked in the way adults expect. The film's Harry is told directly and positioned as cooperative from the start, which slightly softens the sense that he is suppressing dangerous feelings about Black rather than simply being sensibly cautious.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 2 & 3 — Sirius's head in the fire, common room meeting
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, Sirius appears in the fire having broken into a wizarding house to use it. He is warm but urgent, immediately focused on Harry's wellbeing, lets Harry talk himself out before intervening, and then delivers substantive intelligence: Karkaroff's Death Eater history, Moody's attack before term, Bertha Jorkins, the pattern of suspicious events. He also begins to give Harry concrete dragon-fighting advice before being cut off. The scene is long, emotionally rich, and establishes Sirius as Harry's primary adult confidant and strategic advisor.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film condenses the fireplace meeting drastically. Sirius leads with a near-accusatory 'Did you or did you not put your name in the Goblet of Fire?' before softening. The intelligence briefing is reduced to two sentences: Karkaroff was a Death Eater, and Barty Crouch sent his own son to Azkaban. There is no discussion of Bertha Jorkins, no analysis of Moody's attack, no dragon advice, no extended strategic reasoning. The meeting is cut short by Ron entering, and Sirius disappears without the substantive guidance he provides in the book.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's fireplace scene is the central demonstration of Sirius functioning as Harry's godfather-as-mentor: he thinks strategically, gathers intelligence while on the run, and equips Harry to survive. Stripping this to two brief warnings removes Sirius's investigative competence and his primary plot-functional role as Harry's external intelligence source. The accusatory opening ('Did you or did you not...') also introduces a brief note of distrust absent from the book, where Sirius simply lets Harry talk.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 3 — Sirius's line 'You don't have a choice' after Harry says 'I'm not ready for this'
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book Sirius is consistently encouraging and emotionally supportive. He tells Harry 'Dragons we can deal with, Harry' and emphasises that there is a way through every obstacle. His tone is that of someone trying to give Harry confidence and practical tools, not fatalistic resignation. He expresses deep concern but channels it into action.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: When Harry says 'I'm not ready for this, Sirius,' the film Sirius responds flatly: 'You don't have a choice.' This is the last substantive thing he says before being cut off. The line is blunt, offers no comfort, no strategy, no encouragement.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book Sirius actively works to help Harry feel capable and prepared. 'You don't have a choice' is defeatist and cold in a way that contradicts his characterisation as a godfather who deeply wants to protect and empower Harry. It reduces him briefly to a plot-delivery mechanism rather than a caring adult.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 2 — Sirius's letter delivered via owl as a voice-over on the train
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, Sirius's communications are letters carried by tropical birds, carefully worded to avoid interception, and reflect his warmth, care, and caution. Harry's anticipation of Sirius's replies is an emotionally significant thread throughout the early chapters — Harry worries Sirius has been caught, feels relief when letters arrive, and reads them privately with Ron and Hermione. The letters demonstrate ongoing, attentive engagement with Harry's life.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Sirius's letter on the train is delivered as a voice-over, with Sirius's disembodied voice narrating directly to Harry. The content is functional — warning about Ministry owl interception and arranging the fireplace meeting — but the mode of delivery (voice-over rather than a read letter) and the compression into a single moment strips the ongoing epistolary relationship of its texture. There is no sense of Harry anxiously waiting, no warmth in the correspondence, no shared reading with Ron and Hermione.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's letter-writing thread is how the godfather relationship is built across the early part of GoF. Harry's emotional investment in Sirius's safety, his guilt about drawing Sirius back north, and Sirius's attentive replies all develop the bond. Collapsing this into a functional voice-over erases the relational texture that makes Sirius's later appearances meaningful.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 3 — Sirius's absence from the Hogsmeade cave meeting
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book contains an extended cave scene in Hogsmeade where Sirius meets Harry, Ron, and Hermione in person (as a dog, then transforming). He is physically present, eating chicken, pacing, analysing the Crouch situation in detail, discussing Snape's past, warning about Bagman, showing emotional depth (the darkened look when Crouch is mentioned, the bark-laugh about Crouch's son), and demonstrating sharp political intelligence. He also gives Harry direct instructions and expresses paternal concern. The scene runs across many pages and is the fullest in-person portrait of Sirius as godfather and advisor.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The cave meeting is entirely absent from the film corpus. There is no in-person Hogsmeade meeting between Sirius and Harry in the film. All of Sirius's advisory function is compressed into the brief fireplace scene.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The cave scene is the single most important scene for Sirius's characterisation in GoF. It establishes him as politically astute, emotionally complex, physically sacrificing (living as a dog on rats to protect Harry), and genuinely paternally present. It also delivers the Crouch backstory, the Snape/Death Eater discussion, and the Bagman suspicion — all plot-critical intelligence. Its complete absence means the film Sirius has almost no demonstrable competence or depth, and the godfather relationship is reduced to two brief magical communications.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 3 — Sirius absent from Barty Crouch Sr. analysis and political intelligence
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the cave scene, Sirius delivers an extended, nuanced account of Barty Crouch Sr.: his rise, his authoritarian measures, his sending Sirius to Azkaban without trial, his son's imprisonment and death, and his current suspicious behaviour. Sirius speaks from personal experience of injustice and shows both bitterness and analytical clarity. This positions him as someone with hard-won insider knowledge of Ministry corruption.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: In the fireplace scene, Sirius mentions only that 'Barty Crouch sent his own son to Azkaban' as a single characterising data point, with no context, no personal history, no analysis of Crouch's pattern of behaviour. The film Sirius has no demonstrated personal grievance against or knowledge of Crouch beyond this line.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Sirius's knowledge of Crouch is not merely plot exposition — it reflects his personal experience of Ministry injustice and gives him moral authority as a commentator on institutional corruption. Reducing it to one throwaway line removes both characterisation depth and the thematic resonance of Sirius as a victim of the same system that victimised Crouch's son.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 5 (post-second-task) — Sirius entirely absent from Harry's post-task relief and ongoing correspondence
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: After the second task, Harry sends Sirius a detailed account of surviving the dragon and the lake. Sirius sends daily owls as the third task approaches, reminding Harry to focus on survival and not the wider threat of Voldemort. He sends a muddy-paw-print good-luck card on the morning of the third task. This sustained contact demonstrates Sirius's constant vigilance and emotional investment.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film corpus contains no Sirius correspondence after the fireplace scene. There is no post-task letter, no daily owls, no good-luck card. Sirius is absent from the film's second and third act until he appears at the end.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's sustained correspondence in the lead-up to the third task is what makes Sirius's emotional presence felt even when he cannot be physically present. It establishes the godfather bond as active, attentive, and mutual. Its absence means the audience has no basis for understanding the emotional weight of Harry and Sirius's reunion after the graveyard.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 6 — Sirius's role in the post-graveyard hospital wing scene
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, when Dumbledore reveals that there is a large black dog in the pumpkin patch and McGonagall is sent to fetch it, Sirius is then present in Dumbledore's office when Harry arrives. He is described as white and gaunt, crossing the room swiftly, his hands shaking as he helps Harry into a chair. He asks urgently what happened. During Harry's account he grips Harry's shoulder tightly, makes vehement exclamations at the news of Wormtail cutting Harry's arm, and has his face in his hands at the mention of his parents' echoes. He advocates letting Harry rest rather than forcing him to recount immediately. At the end, Dumbledore asks if Sirius would like to stay with Harry in the hospital wing, and Sirius accompanies Harry as the dog, stays through Mrs Weasley's shock, growls at Fudge, and is present when Dumbledore asks him and Snape to shake hands before sending Sirius off to reassemble the Order.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film corpus includes the instruction for McGonagall to fetch the black dog from the pumpkin patch (Scene 6, Dumbledore's lines), confirming Sirius is present. However, the film corpus does not contain the detailed emotional beats of this scene — the swift crossing of the room, the shaking hands, the shoulder grip, the face in hands. The scene is referenced structurally but the emotional texture of Sirius's response to Harry's trauma is not evidenced in the corpus.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's post-graveyard scene is the emotional culmination of the godfather relationship in GoF — Sirius's physical and emotional response to Harry's trauma is the payoff for everything built across the novel. While the film structurally includes Sirius's presence, the corpus does not evidence the detailed emotional beats that make this scene work as relationship culmination. Confidence on this entry is lower given corpus limitations.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 3 — King's Cross platform, Sirius in dog form accompanying Harry to the train
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 326-337: Sirius disobeys Dumbledore's explicit instructions by transforming into a dog and accompanying Harry to King's Cross. Mrs. Weasley is furious ('oh, for heaven's sake, Sirius, Dumbledore said no!'). The moment is bittersweet — Sirius gambolling around, scaring cats, chasing the train — capturing his cabin-fever recklessness, his deep need to be present for Harry, and the poignancy of a man who has almost nothing left clinging to this one act of connection.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film includes Sirius coming to the platform in dog form, but compresses and strips the scene of its emotional texture. Moody's rebuke ('Padfoot, are you barking mad? You'll blow the entire operation') and Sirius's response ('What's life without a little risk?') reduce his motivation to a breezy one-liner. The book's sustained imagery of him bounding alongside the train, the farewell moment of him rearing up on Harry's shoulders, and the genuine tenderness/anxiety layered into the goodbye are collapsed. His dog-form gambolling and the cat-chasing detail that makes his joy so vivid and specific is absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The film retains the basic beat but flattens the emotional register. The book uses this scene to simultaneously show Sirius's recklessness, his desperate need for freedom and connection, and the genuine warmth between him and Harry. Reducing it to a quip ('What's life without a little risk?') tips the portrayal toward glib rather than layered, losing the poignancy of a man who has lost almost everything still reaching out.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 1 — Grimmauld Place kitchen, Sirius at Order meeting / initial reunion with Harry
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 56-96: Sirius's first appearance is physically and emotionally detailed — he is 'panting slightly', sweeping his 'long dark hair' out of his eyes, greeting Harry 'grimly'. The reunion in the kitchen shows him sardonic about his confinement ('Personally, I'd have welcomed a Dementor attack'), warm but hard-edged, clearly suffering from being stuck in the house. He gives Harry a grin that is 'something like' — not a full grin. His bitterness about Snape's reports and the 'cleaning' is specific and character-defining.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: In the film, the initial reunion and kitchen scenes are heavily compressed. Sirius appears briefly before the Order argument. The rich portrait of his confinement-induced bitterness, his sardonic humour about Dementors, his specific complaints about Snape's snide remarks, and the domestic detail of Crookshanks on his lap are all absent. His first substantive dialogue is largely the Order briefing scene and the argument with Molly.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book carefully establishes Sirius's psychological state before any plot function — the cost of his confinement, his self-deprecating dark humour, his complex relationship with the house he hates. The film skips this establishment, so Sirius's later moodiness and recklessness lack the grounded context the book provides. Audiences lose the sense of a man already being slowly hollowed out.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 1 — Grimmauld Place kitchen, the Molly/Sirius argument over telling Harry the truth
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 98-131: This is an extended, carefully staged confrontation. Sirius argues with cool deliberateness and genuine conviction ('He's not a child... He's dealt with as much as most in the Order, and more than some'). His position is philosophically coherent — Harry has earned the right to know. The argument escalates to Sirius rising from his chair before Lupin physically restrains him. Molly's line 'He's not James, Sirius' and Sirius's cold response 'I'm perfectly clear who he is' is a crucial beat establishing the James-confusion subplot. Sirius's face goes white. Lupin's mediation is essential.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film retains the core argument ('He's not your son' / 'He's got me') but significantly compresses it. The key line 'He's not James, Sirius' is delivered by Molly and is present, but the full escalation — Sirius rising, going white, being physically restrained by Lupin — is absent or reduced. Snape's intrusion with 'How touchingly paternal, Black. Perhaps Potter will grow up to be a felon, just like his godfather' replaces some of the emotional complexity with an external jab, and Sirius's response 'You stay out of this, Snivelus' is delivered in a more immediately reactive, less controlled register than the book's cold 'I'm perfectly clear who he is'.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The James-confusion motif is central to understanding Sirius's relationship with Harry and his fatal flaw. The film gestures at it but does not let it breathe. Sirius's controlled anger collapsing into near-violence, then being pulled back — his face going white — shows the specific way confinement and grief have destabilised him. The film's version is more reactive and less psychologically specific, weakening the foundation for the Snape confrontation later and for audience understanding of why Sirius makes fatal choices.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 4 — Gryffindor common room fireplace, Sirius's head appears to talk to Harry, Ron and Hermione
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 396-440: This is a long, rich scene. Sirius appears grinning, proud of the DA idea ('Of course I do! D'you think your father and I would've lain down and taken orders from an old hag like Umbridge?'). He gives useful intelligence about Fudge, about Umbridge's anti-werewolf legislation, about Mundungus being the disguised witch. He suggests the Shrieking Shack, accepts Hermione's rebuttal graciously ('Fair point'). Then comes the pivotal wound: when Harry says they don't want him to come to Hogsmeade, Sirius's face becomes 'a crease between his sunken eyes' and he says 'You're less like your father than I thought... The risk would've been what made it fun for James.' This is a moment of genuine cruelty — Sirius using James as a weapon against Harry out of wounded pride — before lying about Kreacher and vanishing. The 'definite coolness' in his voice is explicit.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film has a fireplace scene but it is heavily compressed. Sirius gives the DA his blessing and provides some intelligence. The critical wound — Sirius telling Harry he is 'less like his father' because Harry won't take a reckless risk — is absent from the film corpus. This specific beat, where Sirius's own need and hurt causes him to strike at Harry in a way that is petty and revealing, is one of his most complex and humanising moments in the book.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The 'less like your father' line is one of the most important characterisation beats for Sirius in the entire novel. It shows he is not simply a noble godfather figure but a damaged man who, when thwarted, can use James's memory as a cudgel. It establishes the James-confusion at its most active and harmful. Its absence makes Sirius's film portrayal significantly more uncomplicated and heroic than the book intends, and removes a layer of tragic self-awareness from his eventual death.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 4 — Grimmauld Place, Sirius/Snape kitchen confrontation over Occlumency
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 640-678: This is a detailed, psychologically loaded confrontation. Sirius is 'louder than ever', asserting ownership of his house against Snape's calm contempt. The confrontation escalates to both men drawing wands, squaring up 'faces barely a foot apart'. Snape's taunt — 'did you know that Lucius Malfoy recognised you last time you risked a little jaunt outside? Clever idea, Black, getting yourself seen on a safe station platform... gave you a cast-iron excuse not to leave your hidey-hole in future' — accusing him of deliberate cowardice — makes Sirius raise his wand. Harry physically gets between them. The aftermath shows Sirius 'glaring', breathing heavily, with 'what looked like an enormous effort' to smile at Mr Weasley. Harry worries Snape has 'stung Sirius so badly he might plan some foolhardy trip'. This directly plants the seed of Sirius's death.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film has the Snape confrontation but compresses it. Sirius's 'You stay out of this, Snivelus' is an early reactive beat. The full escalation — both wands drawn, Harry physically between them, Sirius barely controlling himself, the specific cowardice taunt about the platform that directly motivates his later fatal action — is not present in the film corpus at the level of detail the book provides. The causal chain from Snape's taunt to Sirius leaving Grimmauld Place is not established clearly for the film audience.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This scene is structurally load-bearing. Snape's cowardice taunt is the specific psychological trigger that makes Sirius determined to prove himself by going to the Ministry — it explains his fatal choice. Without this scene's full weight, Sirius's death becomes a contingent tragedy rather than the result of his specific character flaw being exploited. The audience loses the tragic logic of his end: a man goaded by shame into proving he is not a coward.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 4 — Grimmauld Place, Sirius gives Harry the two-way mirror
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 682-685: Sirius quietly gives Harry a badly wrapped package — the two-way mirror — with specific instructions: 'A way of letting me know if Snape's giving you a hard time... I want you to use it if you need me.' Harry privately resolves never to use it because he will not be the one to lure Sirius from safety. This creates a devastating dramatic irony: Harry has the tool to safely contact Sirius throughout the year but never uses it out of protectiveness, meaning the mirror appears only in the heartbreaking coda after Sirius's death.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The two-way mirror and its handover are absent from the film corpus. The mirror does not appear as a plot device or emotional element in the film's version of events. The entire ironic structure — Harry having a safe means of contact and choosing not to use it — is lost.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The two-way mirror is one of the book's most carefully laid tragic ironies. Harry's guilt after Sirius's death is intensified by the knowledge that he had a safe alternative to the Floo Network, but never used it out of love and protectiveness. Its absence collapses this layer of Harry's grief and self-reproach, and removes a key piece of Sirius's characterisation as someone who tried to remain connected to Harry safely. The post-death scene where Harry tries the mirror and it doesn't work — one of the most devastating passages in the corpus — exists in the book but has no setup in the film.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 4 — Gryffindor Common Room fire, second fireplace conversation, Sirius's reaction to Snape stopping Occlumency
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 844-848: When Harry tells Sirius that Snape has stopped his Occlumency lessons, Sirius shouts ('He WHAT?') and actually makes to stand up from the fire, physically moving to go confront Snape at Hogwarts, before Lupin wrenches him back. This shows Sirius's impulsive protectiveness of Harry overriding all practical judgment — exactly the pattern that will kill him.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: This second fireplace conversation and Sirius's explosive reaction to the Occlumency stoppage are not present in the film corpus.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This beat reinforces the specific quality of Sirius's recklessness — it is triggered by protectiveness of Harry, not mere thrill-seeking. It also shows Lupin's repeated role as the person who physically restrains Sirius from self-destruction. Both of these patterns feed directly into the climax. Their absence thins the preparation for Sirius's fatal leap through the veil.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 4 — Grimmauld Place Christmas period, Sirius's moodiness as Harry's departure approaches
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 611-638: The book gives extended attention to Sirius's psychological deterioration as Christmas ends and Harry must return to Hogwarts. He becomes 'moodier and surlier than before', withdrawing to Buckbeak's room, his 'gloom seeping through the house'. This is distinct from his delight when Harry first arrived. Hermione suggests he is 'being selfish' and may be 'confused about whether you're you or your father'. Harry notices Sirius 'singing carols' when the Weasleys arrived, then the contrast as departure nears. This arc — brief happiness, then collapse — is the emotional core of Sirius's story in the book.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film compresses the Christmas period substantially. The emotional arc of Sirius's brief revival followed by deepening gloom as Harry's departure approaches is not sustained. The film has the warm Christmas scene with family gifts and togetherness but does not develop the subsequent deterioration and withdrawal that the book makes central to Sirius's psychological portrait.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's Sirius is not simply a warm, heroic godfather who dies tragically. He is a man being slowly destroyed by confinement, whose brief moments of joy only throw his despair into sharper relief. The film's compression of this arc means Sirius reads as a functional, largely stable character whose death is purely an external event rather than the culmination of an internal disintegration. This significantly reduces the tragedy's depth.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 5 — Department of Mysteries, Sirius calls Harry 'James' at the moment of battle
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 1004: During the battle, Sirius shouts 'Nice one, James!' to Harry after Harry casts a successful spell, then immediately corrects himself. The book does not flag this as a dramatic beat — it is a single line. But it is the culmination of the James-confusion motif that has run through the entire novel, and it occurs at the moment just before Sirius's death.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: In the film corpus (Film Scene 7), Sirius shouts 'Nice one, James!' — this beat IS present in the film. This is one of the faithful moments.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This beat is present in the film and faithfully rendered. No damage score applies — included here only for completeness of analysis. Scoring: 0 damage.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 7 — Department of Mysteries, Sirius's death and Harry's immediate response
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 1010-1029: Sirius's death is preceded by him 'laughing at' Bellatrix — 'Come on, you can do better than that!' — his face showing 'mingled fear and surprise' only as the curse hits. His body 'curved in a graceful arc'. Lupin has to physically drag Harry away, Harry fighting with 'every bit of strength he had'. Harry's refusal to believe it, his conviction that Sirius is 'just behind the curtain', his rage that Sirius is 'keeping him waiting' — this psychological portrait of denial is extended and specific. The moment when Harry realises 'Sirius had never kept him waiting before... Sirius had risked everything, always, to see Harry, to help him' is devastating in its clarity.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film renders Sirius's death visually (the curse, the graceful fall through the veil, Lupin restraining Harry, Harry screaming). However, the internal monologue of denial — the specific thought process by which Harry cannot and then finally must accept it — is necessarily absent as internal narration. More significantly, the film's Sirius does not have the 'laughing at her' moment clearly established before the killing curse lands in a way that the corpus confirms with the same texture.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The film renders the visual event faithfully but cannot fully convey Harry's extended psychological denial, which is where much of the scene's emotional power resides in the book. The loss is inherent to the medium change, but the compression means the death registers as a sudden shock rather than a slow, agonising dawning. This is a moderate damage, not structural.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 4 — Grimmauld Place, Sirius's treatment of Kreacher and the consequences
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 187-203, 248-252, 628-635: The book establishes an extended, specific portrait of Sirius's contemptuous treatment of Kreacher — ordering him around with impatience, threatening him with clothes, eventually throwing him bodily from a room. Hermione repeatedly defends Kreacher. Dumbledore's post-death explanation (Book Scene 1074-1076) explicitly traces Sirius's death back to this neglect: Kreacher's betrayal was enabled by Sirius treating him as 'a servant unworthy of much interest or notice'. The book is unsparing — Sirius's flaw, his inability to see Kreacher as a being with feelings, directly caused his death.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film has Kreacher present and Sirius dismissing him ('Kreacher! That's enough of your bile. Away with you') but the extended pattern of contemptuous treatment, the specific incidents of throwing him out, threatening him, and the explicit causal chain from this neglect to Sirius's death (via Kreacher's betrayal to Narcissa) is not developed. Dumbledore's post-death explanation connecting Sirius's treatment of Kreacher to the fatal trap is absent from the film corpus.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This is one of the book's most important structural elements. Sirius is not merely a victim of Voldemort's cleverness — he is a man whose specific moral failure (inability to extend compassion to a 'lesser' being) directly caused his own death. The film's Sirius dies because Harry is tricked, full stop. The book's Sirius dies because of a chain that runs from his treatment of Kreacher through Kreacher's betrayal to Voldemort's trap. Losing this causation makes Sirius's death a contingency rather than a tragedy with moral weight, and removes one of the book's central thematic statements about the cost of contempt.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 4 — Grimmauld Place drawing room, Black family tapestry scene
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 204-242: Extended scene in which Sirius shows Harry the Black family tapestry, explaining his own history — running away at 16, living at the Potters', his Uncle Alphard's gold, Regulus's death, Bellatrix, Andromeda. He opens up about hating his family, smiles 'bitterly', runs fingers through his 'long, unkempt hair'. The scene ends with him confessing 'I don't like being back here... I never thought I'd be stuck in this house again' and Harry understanding completely by analogy to Privet Drive. Sirius's personal history, his relationship to the house as a place of trauma, and his genuine interiority are all given space here.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film has the Black family tree scene (Sirius explains his mother blasting him off, going to Harry's dad's) but it is significantly compressed. The emotional confession at the end — 'I don't like being back here' — and Harry's empathetic understanding are reduced or absent. The specific details about Regulus, Andromeda, and the texture of Sirius's family history receive less development.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The tapestry scene is where Sirius becomes most fully a person rather than a plot function. Its compression means the audience's understanding of why Grimmauld Place is specifically tormenting for Sirius — not just confining, but returning him to the site of his original oppression — is attenuated. This matters for the emotional logic of his deterioration throughout the story.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 4 — Umbridge's office fireplace, Sirius's response to Harry's account of the Pensieve scene
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 817-842: When Harry tells Sirius and Lupin what he saw in the Pensieve — James bullying Snape — Sirius's response is carefully calibrated. He tries to excuse James ('James was everything Snape wanted to be'), admits 'I'm not proud of it', accepts being called 'arrogant little berks', laughs affectionately at the memory of James messing his hair, and delivers the crucial defence: 'your father was the best friend I ever had and he was a good person. A lot of people are idiots at the age of fifteen. He grew out of it.' This is a portrait of Sirius as someone capable of honest self-assessment about his own youthful cruelty while still defending James with genuine love.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: This entire scene — Harry contacting Sirius from Umbridge's office to discuss the Pensieve, Sirius and Lupin's joint response, the honest admission of past cruelty and the defence of James — is absent from the film. The Pensieve scene itself is shown but Harry does not seek Sirius's counsel about it.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This is one of the most important scenes for the Harry-Sirius relationship in the entire book. Sirius functions here as the person who helps Harry reconcile his idealized image of his father with the ugly reality, and does so with honesty and love. His ability to say 'we were arrogant little berks' while still saying 'he was the best friend I ever had' is a portrait of mature, unsentimental love. Its absence means a significant dimension of both Sirius's character and his relationship with Harry is entirely missing from the film.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 4 (Slughorn's house) - Slughorn mentions Regulus Black photo, describes Sirius as simply 'died a few weeks ago'
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 46-47: Slughorn describes Sirius as 'a big pal of your father's at school,' emphasizes his exceptional talent ('he was a talented boy'), notes the anomaly of a Black in Gryffindor with genuine warmth and collector's regret. The passage conveys Sirius as a figure of real distinction and personal connection to Harry's father's world. Harry's visceral reaction ('as though an invisible hand had twisted Harry's intestines') underscores the emotional weight Sirius carries.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 4: Slughorn's mention of Sirius is extremely brief and clinical — 'You no doubt know of his older brother Sirius. Died a few weeks ago. I taught the whole Black family except Sirius. Shame. Talented boy. I got Regulus when he came along, of course, but I'd have liked the set.' The remark is delivered as a throwaway line while Slughorn is distracted by Harry, with no pause for Harry's reaction, no emotional weight, and no establishment of Sirius as a figure connected to Harry's father or to Harry's grief.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book uses this Slughorn moment to ambush Harry — and the audience — with a casual reminder of Sirius's death that lands like a gut punch precisely because it comes from an outsider who doesn't know the weight of what he's saying. The film compresses this to a perfunctory aside, losing both the establishment of Sirius as a figure of real distinction in the wizarding world and the opportunity to show Harry's raw, unprocessed grief triggered by an unexpected mention of his godfather's name. This weakens the ongoing emotional throughline of Harry carrying Sirius's loss.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 4 (Slughorn's house) - No Harry grief reaction to Sirius mention
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 46: Harry's reaction to Slughorn's casual mention of Sirius is described as 'as though an invisible hand had twisted Harry's intestines and held them tight' — a visceral, physical grief response. Book Scenes 52-57 further establish Harry's ongoing devastation: Dumbledore notes 'it is cruel that you and Sirius had such a short time together,' Harry admits 'it's just hard to realize he won't write to me again,' and Harry's resolution to honor Sirius by fighting on is framed as a direct emotional consequence of his grief.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film provides no visible reaction from Harry to Slughorn's mention of Sirius. The screenplay describes Harry as distracted by looking at the photograph of Regulus (who resembles Sirius), but there is no internal grief beat, no pause, no emotional register of loss comparable to the book's 'invisible hand' moment.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Harry's grief over Sirius is a foundational emotional arc at the opening of Half-Blood Prince. The book carefully charts how Harry is haunted by Sirius's loss throughout the summer and early school year — it motivates his recklessness, his relationship with Dumbledore's private lessons, and his defiant resolve. Removing the emotional gut-punch reaction from this early scene cuts the audience off from understanding Harry's internal state and strips the Sirius arc of one of its most effective early beats.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film — absent scene: Dumbledore's conversation with Harry outside the Burrow (broomstick shed)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 52-57: Dumbledore explicitly honors Sirius in a private conversation with Harry, saying 'I think Sirius would have been proud of you,' acknowledging 'it was cruel that you and Sirius had such a short time together. A brutal ending to what should have been a long and happy relationship.' Harry confesses 'it's just hard to realize he won't write to me again' and articulates that Sirius was 'almost like a parent' — the best thing about discovering his godfather. Dumbledore responds: 'Sirius represented much to you that you had never known before.' The scene ends with Dumbledore calling Harry 'Sirius's true godson.' This is the primary direct eulogy for Sirius in the book and the scene where Harry's grief is most fully articulated.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: No equivalent scene appears in the film corpus. The film skips directly from Slughorn's house to Hogwarts without any private Dumbledore-Harry conversation that addresses Sirius's death, Harry's grief, or the significance of what Sirius meant to Harry as a parent figure.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This is the single most damaging absence in the corpus. The broomstick shed conversation is the book's emotional keystone for the Sirius arc in HBP — it is where Harry processes his loss out loud for the first time, where Dumbledore validates Sirius's importance as a parental figure, and where Harry's grief is transformed into defiant resolve ('I'll make sure I take as many Death Eaters with me as I can'). Dumbledore calling him 'Sirius's true godson' is a direct passing of the torch. Without this scene, Sirius's death lacks a proper emotional reckoning in the adaptation, Harry's grief arc is truncated, and the thematic connection between losing Sirius and Harry's readiness to sacrifice himself is severed.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film — absent scene: Sirius's will, inheritance of Grimmauld Place, and Kreacher transfer
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 25-36: Sirius leaves Harry everything — gold, Grimmauld Place, Buckbeak, and Kreacher. Harry's reaction to inheriting Grimmauld Place is deeply emotional: 'He never wanted to set foot in number twelve, Grimmauld Place again if he could help it. He thought he would be haunted forever by the memory of Sirius prowling its dark musty rooms alone, imprisoned within the place he had wanted so desperately to leave.' The inheritance establishes Sirius's final act of trust in Harry and forces Harry to take responsibility for Kreacher — the creature who betrayed Sirius — demonstrating Harry's moral growth. The scene also establishes Bellatrix as the alternative heir, directly connecting Sirius's death to ongoing plot stakes.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: No equivalent scene appears in the film corpus. There is no handling of Sirius's will, inheritance, Grimmauld Place ownership, or Kreacher's transfer to Harry's ownership.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Sirius's will is one of his most important post-death narrative functions. It makes him an active presence even after death, forcing Harry into a relationship with his legacy, his home, and the creature who helped cause his death. Harry's decision to send Kreacher to Hogwarts rather than let him go to Bellatrix is a significant moral and practical choice. The absence of all this removes Sirius's continued narrative agency and a key dimension of Harry's emotional processing of the loss — the painful reality of inheriting the prison Sirius could never escape.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film — absent scene: Mundungus stealing from Grimmauld Place / Harry's fury at Sirius's possessions being taken
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 133-140: Harry confronts Mundungus in Hogsmeade after catching him selling items stolen from Sirius's house, including pieces with the Black family crest. Harry's rage — 'He's nicked Sirius's stuff! Nicked it!' — and his continued fuming over it with Ron and Hermione ('Harry was thinking about Sirius, and how he had hated those silver goblets anyway') shows his ongoing protective attachment to Sirius's memory and possessions. Dumbledore later confirms he is aware of the theft and assures Harry it will stop (Scene 148).
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: No equivalent scene involving Mundungus stealing Sirius's possessions appears in the film corpus.
damaging_scenes.explanation: While not a major structural scene, the Mundungus confrontation is one of the few moments in HBP where Harry actively engages with Sirius's memory and legacy in an emotionally charged way outside of private reflection. Its absence further reduces the presence of Sirius's ongoing influence on Harry's emotional life in the adaptation. The scene also serves a practical function, as Mundungus and his theft of Black family heirlooms becomes significant in Deathly Hallows.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 4 (Slughorn's house) - Sirius characterized as 'Regulus's older brother' rather than Harry's godfather and James's best friend
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 47: Slughorn frames Sirius specifically as 'a big pal of your father's at school' — the emphasis is on Sirius's bond with James Potter and by extension with Harry's family history. The phrase 'I'd have liked the set' refers to the collector's regret of a teacher who knew the whole Black family. Sirius is presented as someone who defied his family's expectations by landing in Gryffindor, a sign of his character.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 4: The screenplay has Slughorn introduce Sirius through his relationship to Regulus — 'You no doubt know of his older brother Sirius' — framing Sirius as a secondary figure relative to his younger brother in Slughorn's orbit, rather than as James Potter's best friend and Harry's godfather. The relational framing reverses the book's emphasis.
damaging_scenes.explanation: A minor but telling reversal: the book anchors Sirius to Harry's emotional world (friend of James, effectively family) while the film anchors him to the Black family lineage through Regulus. This subtly reframes Sirius as a peripheral figure in Harry's life story rather than a central one at the very moment his name is first raised in the film.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film — absent scene: Harry's thoughts about Snape's role in Sirius's death / Harry blaming Snape
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 105-106: Harry has spent the summer concluding that 'Snape's snide remarks to Sirius about remaining safely hidden while the rest of the Order of the Phoenix were off fighting Voldemort had probably been a powerful factor in Sirius rushing off to the Ministry the night that he had died.' Harry 'clung to this notion, because it enabled him to blame Snape, which felt satisfying, and also because he knew that if anyone was not sorry that Sirius was dead, it was the man now striding next to him.' This establishes Harry's psychological state regarding Sirius — his guilt displaced as anger at Snape — and drives his hostility toward Snape throughout HBP.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: No equivalent internal monologue or scene establishing Harry's belief that Snape contributed to Sirius's death appears in the film corpus. The film does not establish this specific psychological motivation for Harry's hatred of Snape.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Harry's conviction that Snape goaded Sirius to his death is a key psychological driver of their antagonistic relationship in HBP and gives Harry's hatred a specific, grief-rooted dimension beyond general dislike. It also adds moral complexity — Harry's grief has curdled into a need to blame someone — that enriches his characterization. Removing this motivation flattens both the Sirius grief arc and the Harry-Snape dynamic, making Harry's hostility toward Snape seem more generalized and less emotionally grounded.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film — absent scene: Tonks's grief over Sirius's death affecting her Metamorphosing abilities
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 65-67: Hermione explains that Tonks has been deeply affected by Sirius's death — she feels responsible because she was fighting Bellatrix when Sirius was killed. Her grief has been so profound that it has disrupted her Metamorphosing abilities, which is presented as an unusual and significant manifestation of magical trauma. Harry later observes Tonks directly (Scene 98-99) and notes she is 'older and much more serious and purposeful,' thinking uncomfortably about whether he should say something consoling about Sirius. Harry speculates (Scenes 190-192) that Tonks may have been in love with Sirius, triggered by her near-tears at his name.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: No scene in the film corpus establishes Tonks's grief over Sirius, her disrupted Metamorphosing powers, or Harry's observation of her changed demeanor in connection to Sirius's death.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Tonks's grief arc, while secondary, serves multiple functions: it shows the ripple effect of Sirius's death on people who loved him, it humanizes the Order members as people with emotional lives, and it sets up Harry's speculation about a possible romantic connection between Tonks and Sirius that adds retrospective depth to both characters. Its absence reduces the breadth of Sirius's impact on the world around Harry.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 17 (Astronomy Tower) - Snape's line 'I gave my word. I made a vow' without any established connection to Sirius or the Unbreakable Vow context from the book's opening
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 15-20: The Unbreakable Vow Snape makes to Narcissa includes the clause that he will 'carry out the deed that the Dark Lord has assigned to Draco.' Snape's line on the tower — 'I gave my word. I made a vow' — directly references this vow. Separately, Scene 16 establishes that Snape 'certainly helped dispose of Sirius Black' according to Bellatrix, connecting Snape's role in Sirius's death to the broader context of his treachery. While the Unbreakable Vow scenes are in both book and film corpus by reference, Sirius's death is named as part of Snape's history of serving Voldemort in this same context.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 17: Snape says 'I gave my word. I made a vow' but the audience lacks the book's framing that Snape's betrayals — including his role in Sirius's death — are part of the same pattern of calculated service to Voldemort. The film presents this moment without the loaded history the book has built regarding Snape's culpability in Sirius's fate.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Minor damage: the book's Book Scene 16 explicitly names Sirius's death as something Snape 'helped' bring about, which gives additional weight to Harry's fury on the tower and to the revelation of Snape as the killer. Without this established connection, the audience loses a layer of the Harry-Snape confrontation's emotional logic as it relates to Sirius.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film — absent scene: Dumbledore's funeral / Harry's reflection on never having attended a funeral for Sirius
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 279: 'Harry had never attended a funeral before; there had been no body to bury when Sirius had died.' This line explicitly connects Dumbledore's funeral to the unresolved grief of Sirius's death — Harry was denied the ritual of mourning for his godfather. Book Scene 280 adds: 'Admittedly he had not, as he had with Sirius, looked desperately for some kind of loophole, some way that Dumbledore would come back.' The comparison between the two losses clarifies how Harry has processed (or not) each death.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: While the film corpus includes the aftermath of Dumbledore's death (Scenes 19-20), there is no equivalent moment where Harry explicitly reflects on having been denied a funeral for Sirius or draws a comparative emotional parallel between the two losses.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's funeral scene explicitly invokes Sirius's death as an unresolved grief that shapes how Harry experiences Dumbledore's funeral differently. The absence of this reflection loses a moment where Sirius's presence — or rather his absence from proper mourning — continues to haunt the story's emotional landscape. It also removes a key marker of Harry's psychological progress: he does not seek a loophole for Dumbledore the way he desperately did for Sirius, suggesting growth through grief.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 32 (Forbidden Forest) / Film Scene 33 (Clearing) — Sirius appears via Resurrection Stone
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book scenes 340, 344, 349, 353: Sirius appears tall, handsome, younger than Harry ever saw him in life, loping with easy grace, hands in pockets, grinning. He is actively present, walks beside Harry as a companion and source of courage through the forest, and speaks with characteristic lightness ('Quicker than falling asleep'). He confirms 'We are part of you' and 'Invisible to anyone else.' His presence, along with James, Lupin, and Lily, is described as Harry's courage itself — they march together through the forest. Sirius is portrayed as warm, self-possessed, and emotionally sustaining.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 32: Sirius appears but is given only two short lines — 'Quicker than falling asleep' (in response to Harry asking if dying hurts) and a near-silent gesture pointing to Harry's heart when Harry asks if Voldemort will be able to see them. He does not speak during the walk through the forest. His grin and easy physical grace are present but his characterful voice and active companionship are reduced to near-silence. The book's extended walk with the dead, in which all four figures are described as marching alongside Harry and acting as Patronuses against the Dementors, is compressed; the film cuts almost directly to the clearing after the stone is turned.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Sirius's defining trait in this scene — the easy, slightly careless courage and warmth that Harry has idealized throughout the saga — is present only as a visual impression. The line he does deliver is faithful, but the loss of his active participation in the walk and the reduction of his dialogue to a gesture removes the specific emotional texture the books give him here. Minor damage because the scene as a whole functions and Sirius is visually present, but the characterization is thinned.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 3 (Sirius's room, Grimmauld Place) — Harry in Sirius's bedroom
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book scenes 53–68: Harry enters Sirius's room and spends extended time there. The room is described in vivid detail — Gryffindor banners, Muggle motorcycle posters, bikini-clad Muggle girl posters, all as deliberate provocations to his family. Harry reads a Marauders photograph showing Sirius as 'carelessly handsome, his slightly arrogant face so much younger and happier than Harry had ever seen it alive.' Harry finds and reads Lily's letter, discovers the partial photograph of baby Harry on a toy broomstick, and searches desperately for the letter's missing second page. The room is a rich portrait of who Sirius was as a teenager — his rebellion, his humor, his loyalty — and Harry's emotional engagement with it is substantial.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 3: Harry enters the room and lingers briefly by the Marauders photograph, traces faces with his wand, notices A History of Magic by Bathilda Bagshot, and finds Lily's letter. The room itself is ransacked and shown from a low, slightly unsettling POV (Kreacher's). The distinctive details that characterize teenage Sirius — Gryffindor banners as an act of defiance, motorcycle posters, the bikini posters described as a deliberate nerve — are absent from the screenplay as written. Harry's search for the second page of the letter, which shows his desperate desire to hold onto Sirius, is absent; he simply turns it over, finds no more, and is interrupted by Hermione.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book uses Sirius's teenage bedroom as a retroactive character portrait — the only extended window into who Sirius was before Azkaban, his wit, his deliberate rebelliousness, his joy. The film collapses this to a plot-functional scene (find the letter, learn about Bathilda). The loss of the room's characterizing details and Harry's emotional search removes a significant piece of posthumous characterization that the books use to deepen Harry's grief and the audience's understanding of Sirius as a full person rather than a tragic absence.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 6 (Kitchen, Grimmauld Place) — Kreacher interrogation and the absence of Sirius/Kreacher backstory
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book scenes 88–116: After summoning Kreacher, Harry confronts him about Sirius's betrayal ('you betrayed Sirius to Voldemort'). Kreacher tells the full story of Regulus and Voldemort's cave at length. Hermione delivers her moral argument that 'Sirius was horrible to Kreacher' and that 'Voldemort did… and so did Sirius.' Harry recalls Dumbledore's words: 'I do not think Sirius ever saw Kreacher as a being with feelings as acute as a human's.' The scene establishes that Sirius's own cruelty to Kreacher contributed causally to his death — a morally complex indictment of a character Harry loves, and a direct thematic statement about the treatment of house-elves.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 6: Harry interrogates Kreacher about the locket and Regulus, but the scene is compressed. Kreacher confirms Regulus ordered him to destroy the locket and that Mundungus took it. There is no extended account of Kreacher's ordeal in the cave, no Hermione speech about Sirius's cruelty, and no acknowledgment of the causal link between Sirius's mistreatment of Kreacher and Sirius's death. Harry simply sends Kreacher to find Mundungus. The moral complexity — Sirius partly responsible for his own death through his behavior — is entirely absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This is one of the book's most pointed retrospective characterizations of Sirius: his flaw (inability to see house-elves as fully feeling beings) contributed causally to his death, and Hermione explicitly names this. Removing it not only strips a moral dimension from Sirius's character but eliminates the thematic through-line about house-elf treatment that runs from Chamber of Secrets through this moment. The adaptation loses the acknowledgment that Sirius, for all his courage and loyalty, had a blind spot serious enough to get him killed — a nuance that makes him a more fully human figure.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 20 (Shell Cottage parlor) — Mirror shard explanation
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book scene 209: Harry carries the shard of Sirius's enchanted mirror in his mokeskin pouch alongside the Marauder's Map and other prized objects. The mirror is established in Deathly Hallows book as one of the items Harry values most, a relic of Sirius and the only direct communication channel Sirius once offered him. Its presence throughout the Horcrux hunt is a quiet, persistent marker of Harry's grief and his continued relationship with Sirius's memory.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 21 (cliff by Dobby's grave): Ron asks about the mirror shard and Harry explains, 'Sirius gave it to me. He had a matching piece. He said if I ever needed him, all I had to do was look into it… He died before I ever got to use it.' This is a faithful line, but the framing adds a new element — Harry says he thinks he has seen Dumbledore in it, redirecting the shard's emotional significance away from Sirius and toward Dumbledore/Aberforth. The mirror becomes primarily a plot device for reaching Aberforth rather than a grief-object associated with Sirius.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Minor damage. The film handles the mirror accurately in functional terms and Harry's explanation of Sirius's gift is faithful. However, the reframing of the shard as 'I think I've seen Dumbledore' slightly dilutes its identity as a Sirius-grief object. The impact is low because the scene still acknowledges Sirius and the damage is one of emphasis rather than distortion.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 29 (Great Hall, Snape's memories) — Young Sirius at the Sorting
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book scene 310–322: On the Hogwarts Express, young Sirius is introduced questioning his family's Slytherin tradition with easy confidence — 'Maybe I'll break the tradition. Where are you heading, if you've got the choice?' He is witty ('Where are you hoping to go, seeing as you're neither?'), quick, and already marked as someone charming enough to win James's immediate friendship. At the Sorting, Harry sees Sirius make room for Lily at the Gryffindor table. These moments establish Sirius in youth as confident, funny, slightly arrogant, and magnetically social.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 29: The Sorting scene shows two boys — identified as Sirius Black and James Potter — sitting together at the Gryffindor table. James watches Lily and nudges Sirius to make room for her. There is no dialogue for young Sirius; no train scene; none of the wit or characterization from the book's version of events. Sirius is present as a background figure identified by a stage direction.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The film corpus includes this scene only as a visual beat in Snape's memories, which are focused on Lily and Snape rather than on Sirius. Young Sirius's personality as established in the books is not represented. However, given that this scene belongs to Snape's memory sequence and Sirius is genuinely peripheral to that narrative, the damage is minimal — the scene's purpose is not to characterize Sirius.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 15 (Lovegood house) — Resurrection Stone discussion, Sirius named
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book scene 216: Harry explicitly names Sirius first when discussing who he would bring back with the Resurrection Stone — 'we could have Sirius…Mad-Eye…Dumbledore…my parents.' The order and the specificity of naming Sirius first reflects the primacy of that loss in Harry's emotional landscape throughout the book.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 15: Harry says 'Well, you could bring people back, couldn't you? Mad-Eye. Dumbledore. Sirius. Anybody.' The order places Sirius third, after Mad-Eye and Dumbledore. This is a minor reordering but Sirius is still named.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Negligible damage. Sirius is named and the emotional logic is preserved. The reordering is not meaningfully harmful to the adaptation's portrayal of Sirius's importance to Harry.
